title: Lecture 05 (Lecture 03) - Relational databases, pessimistic locking (airline check-in demo) and a key-value store on a relational database

questions.q: What three items were on the lecture's agenda, in the order written on the board?
questions.answer: Relational databases & pessimistic locking; designing an airline check-in system (live demo of locking); designing a key-value store on a relational DB.

questions.q: What pattern did the teacher say every new foundational technology follows, and what examples did he give?
questions.answer: Its first set of applications is always in finance/accounting: early computers ran spreadsheets/ledgers for accounting; blockchain's first applications were around money; relational databases (rows and columns) were likewise conceived to make financial applications possible.

questions.q: Why did relational databases have to provide very strong guarantees, and which property became their core?
questions.answer: Because they were built to deal with money: you cannot lose a transaction, data must be correct and never corrupted, and multiple people must be able to update it. So ACID and transactions became the core component of relational databases.

questions.q: According to the board, how is data represented in a relational database, what is its key highlight, and what is it known for?
questions.answer: Data is stored and represented in rows and columns; the key highlight is relations (you pick relational databases for relations); they are known for ACID.

questions.q: What trade-off of database indexes was written on the board?
questions.answer: Indexes make reads faster and writes slower.

questions.q: What is the core idea of pessimistic locking, and what is the typical flow written on the board, in order?
questions.answer: You acquire the lock before proceeding. Flow: ACQ_LOCK() -> READ / UPDATE (the critical section) -> REL_LOCK(). Other transactions wait to acquire the lock and can proceed only after it is released.

questions.q: Using the Medium clap-count example, why do we need locking?
questions.answer: If two transactions both do count++ at the same time, both may read the same old value and the final value becomes count+1 instead of count+2 (count++ is not atomic). Locks protect the sanity of the data (consistency and integrity) against concurrent updates.

questions.q: Locking lowers throughput. When is it worth taking locks and when can you skip them?
questions.answer: Take locks where the correctness/sanity of the data is more important than throughput, so the database moves from one correct state to another. In use cases where correctness is not important, it is okay to skip locking.

questions.q: Describe the transactional deadlock drawn on the board (D-01): who holds what and who waits for what?
questions.answer: T1 holds Row 2 and wants a lock on Row 1; Row 1 is held by T2, which wants Row 2. The arrows form a cycle T1 -> Row 1 -> T2 -> Row 2 -> T1, so no one moves forward. Pessimistic locking always risks such a deadlock.

questions.q: What did the teacher advise you to check whenever you write code or SQL that takes locks?
questions.answer: Always check whether it can lead to a deadlock; arrange your statements and the order of lock acquisition and release so it cannot, and if it can, protect against it. Transactional deadlocks are killers: they stall the database.

questions.q: How do databases such as MySQL, Postgres and Oracle avoid entering a deadlock, and which transaction gets killed?
questions.answer: Every time a row lock is requested, the database runs a deadlock detection algorithm (a cyclic path = deadlock). If granting the lock would form a cycle, the transaction requesting that lock (the one firing the query) is killed by the engine. The transaction that detects the deadlock kills itself; the cycle edge is never allowed to form.

questions.q: Why does a database never let itself actually enter a deadlock state?
questions.answer: In a deadlock everything is stalled and nothing moves forward; the only way to recover would be to reboot the database, which means downtime.

questions.q: How can you reproduce the database's deadlock protection locally?
questions.answer: Start two transactions on two rows, have each acquire a lock on one row, then have each request the other's row; the transaction that fires the final locking query is killed.

questions.q: What other names do shared locks and exclusive locks have, and which SQL suffix takes each?
questions.answer: Shared lock = read lock, taken by ending a SELECT with FOR SHARE. Exclusive lock = write lock, taken by ending a SELECT with FOR UPDATE.

questions.q: List the four rules of shared locks written on the board.
questions.answer: 1. Reserved for read by the current transaction; 2. other transactions can read the locked rows; 3. other transactions cannot modify the locked rows; 4. if the current transaction wants to modify, its lock is upgraded to an exclusive lock.

questions.q: In the FOR SHARE example, T1 locks user_id IN (1,2,6) and T2 locks user_id IN (3,4,6). What can each transaction do, and what happens if T2 tries to update?
questions.answer: Both obtain shared locks (row 6 is shared by both). T1 can read and modify (READ & MODIFY); T2 can read but, if it tries to update, it must wait (READ & WAIT) because T1 holds a lock on row 6, until T1 commits or aborts.

questions.q: What is the benefit of using shared locks?
questions.answer: Very high read throughput: other transactions are still allowed to read the locked rows; only modification is blocked.

questions.q: What happens when a transaction holding a shared (read) lock on a row then modifies that row?
questions.answer: The read lock is elevated to an exclusive lock, implicitly (you do nothing), and only then does the modification happen; any update needs an exclusive lock.

questions.q: What are the rules of an exclusive lock as written on the board?
questions.answer: Reserved for write by the current transaction; other transactions cannot read the locked rows; other transactions cannot modify the locked rows.

questions.q: With FOR UPDATE, T1 holds rows (1,2,6). What happens to T2's SELECT ... WHERE user_id IN (3,4,6) FOR UPDATE, and what if T2 had asked only for rows 3 and 4?
questions.answer: T2's query does not even complete: it waits (WAIT) because row 6 is exclusively locked by T1, until T1 commits or aborts. With only 3 and 4 it would have completed immediately.

questions.q: What is the cost of exclusive locks, and when do you still use them?
questions.answer: They severely impact throughput because others cannot even read the locked rows; you use them where you need exclusivity to ensure correctness under concurrent transactions.

questions.q: What does SKIP LOCKED do, and in the (3,4,6) example which rows would T2 get?
questions.answer: It removes locked rows from the result set: on a best-effort basis, rows locked by another transaction are skipped and the query proceeds without waiting. T2 would get only rows 3 and 4.

questions.q: When is SKIP LOCKED not acceptable?
questions.answer: When the use case needs all the requested rows (e.g. all three); then you have to wait, there is no other option.

questions.q: What does NOWAIT do, and what error did the board show?
questions.answer: The locking read does not wait for the lock: if any requested row is locked by another transaction, it fails immediately (the transaction is killed), e.g. ERROR 3572: DO NOT WAIT FOR LOCK. You may then retry, depending on your business.

questions.q: Why does NOWAIT exist instead of always waiting for the lock?
questions.answer: Waiting (e.g. up to a 10-second SQL timeout) needlessly chokes the database's performance for that thread and makes the client wait; if another transaction already locked the row and will process it, there is no reason to wait, so fail at once.

questions.q: What learning approach did the teacher highlight with the airline check-in demo?
questions.answer: Don't build the entire system; implement only the core part you want to understand (here the database locking) as a small prototype, instead of writing CRUD or drawing high-level boxes. Implementing is where the deep insights come from.

questions.q: List the airline check-in system's assumptions written on the board.
questions.answer: Multiple airlines; every airline has multiple planes (flights); each flight has 120 seats; every flight has multiple trips; a user books a seat in one trip of a flight; handle multiple people trying to pick seats on the plane.

questions.q: Which five tables make up the check-in schema (D-04), and how are they linked?
questions.answer: airlines(id, name); flights(id, airline_id, name); trips(id, flight_id, fly_time); users(id, name); seats(id, name, trip_id, user_id). flights.airline_id -> airlines, trips.flight_id -> flights, seats.trip_id -> trips, seats.user_id -> users; user_id is null until someone picks the seat.

questions.q: Describe the high-level architecture of the check-in system (D-05) and what the admin service does.
questions.answer: Users -> check-in service -> MySQL; a separate Admin Svc (used by an admin) also writes to MySQL. The admin service adds new flights and trips and keeps them updated; for every trip it creates one seat row per seat with user_id null.

questions.q: What concurrency scenario was the demo built to handle?
questions.answer: All 120 passengers of the same trip reach the airport at the exact same moment and, at 120 kiosks, try to pick a seat at the same time.

questions.q: What does the check-in demo deliberately not handle?
questions.answer: Reservation and payment: people have already booked and paid for the flight; the demo is only about picking a seat.

questions.q: Why was the demo written in Go, and what would you need otherwise?
questions.answer: For simplicity, elegance and easy concurrency (goroutines). Any language works if it supports concurrency; otherwise you'd need multiple processes to mimic concurrent users.

questions.q: What does approach 0 do, and what is wrong with it?
questions.answer: One user (passed as an argument) is asked which seat to book; in a transaction it runs UPDATE seats SET user_id = ? WHERE id = ? and commits. There are zero checks, so another user can book the exact same seat (last one wins).

questions.q: What changes in approach 1 and why does it still fail?
questions.answer: Instead of the user choosing, the code picks a seat at random from all seats of the plane (not just available ones) and updates it, still with no checks. The random function can pick the same seat twice, so two people can get the same seat.

questions.q: How does approach 2 simulate the 120 passengers, and what was the result?
questions.answer: It starts one goroutine per user (120) at the same time, each picking a random seat and updating it. Result: not all seats were filled, because the random function repeated values, so several users got the same seat (e.g. two users each booked 7-E and 12-E).

questions.q: What query does approach 3 use to pick a seat?
questions.answer: SELECT id, name, trip_id, user_id FROM seats WHERE trip_id = 1 AND user_id IS NULL ORDER BY id LIMIT 1, then UPDATE that seat and commit, run by 120 goroutines in parallel.

questions.q: Approach 3 checks user_id IS NULL. Why do many users still get the same seat?
questions.answer: The transactions run at the exact same time with no lock, so they all see the same old value (the seat still null) and all operate on it; this is exactly why locking is needed.

questions.q: In approach 3, why does everyone get specifically the first free seat?
questions.answer: Because of ORDER BY id (LIMIT 1): every concurrent transaction is handed the lowest-id free seat (seat 1A first).

questions.q: What did approach 3 actually produce over several runs?
questions.answer: Only a handful of seats filled per run (two, three or four, in order 1A, 1B, 1C...), with almost all users assigned the same seat; there is no guarantee of exactly n seats.

questions.q: Why did approach 3 still fill more than one seat?
questions.answer: Some goroutines started their transaction after an earlier one had already committed; their read then saw that seat's user_id as not null and picked the next one. That is due to the commit plus the user_id IS NULL condition, not to any locking in the code.

questions.q: What exactly changed from approach 3 to approach 4?
questions.answer: Only two words added at the end of the select: FOR UPDATE (... ORDER BY id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE), taking an exclusive lock on the selected seat row.

questions.q: A student predicted approach 4 would deadlock. How did the teacher correct this?
questions.answer: Waiting is not deadlock. A deadlock happens when you wait on a row locked by someone who is in turn waiting on a row you hold; in approach 4 transactions just wait for one lock.

questions.q: Asked 'aren't ACID properties given by default, so why lock?', what did the teacher answer?
questions.answer: ACID is at the transaction level; how concurrent transactions are scheduled depends on the isolation level (read uncommitted, read committed, repeatable read, serializable). Locking is something you do within a transaction to coordinate concurrent transactions on rows.

questions.q: Would the serializable isolation level solve the seat problem, and why isn't it used?
questions.answer: Yes: serializable executes transactions one after another, so the problem would not occur, but it is pathetically slow. It is not the default and not used because you need high throughput and parallel writes (a writer of row 100 should not wait for a writer of row 1).

questions.q: The teacher asked how a database could just 'move to the next row' when the first is locked. What was his point about a pointed query like WHERE id = 67?
questions.answer: The database must handle all query shapes uniformly; for a pointed row lock like id = 67 it cannot move to another row. So rows are not handed out by 'jumping' to the next row; instead waiting transactions re-evaluate the query after the lock is released.

questions.q: What was the result of running approach 4 (FOR UPDATE)?
questions.answer: All 120 seats filled on every run, assigned in seat order (1A, 1B, 1C ... 20F), taking about 1.2 to 1.8 seconds.

questions.q: Explain what the database does in approach 4 when 120 transactions run the same FOR UPDATE query.
questions.answer: One transaction locks the first free row; the others see the row they are iterating over is locked and wait (they do not get the row). When the holder commits or aborts, the waiting transactions are signalled and re-evaluate the same query (the client does not re-fire it); one of them gets the next free row and locks it, and so on.

questions.q: In approach 4, does user 1 get seat 1, user 2 seat 2, and so on?
questions.answer: No. Seats fill in seat order, but whichever transaction gets scheduled first gets the next seat, so the user-to-seat mapping is not in user order.

questions.q: What is the cost of approach 4, even though it is correct?
questions.answer: It is painful for the database: after every commit all waiting transactions are signalled and re-evaluate, one succeeding at a time, so it is slow; but correctness is guaranteed.

questions.q: What is the change in approach 5, and what was its measured effect?
questions.answer: Adding SKIP LOCKED (... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED). All 120 seats were still filled, in 147 ms instead of about 1.7 s: roughly a tenth of the time.

questions.q: With SKIP LOCKED, what does the database do when the second transaction finds the first row locked?
questions.answer: It still takes exclusive locks, but it skips the locked row and takes the next row matching the WHERE clause; no transaction waits for another to complete, so rows are locked continuously in parallel.

questions.q: What did the teacher say about the claim that 'relational databases don't scale'?
questions.answer: It is wrong: relational databases scale beautifully and are champions at handling high QPS; you just need to know performance tuning (here just normal SQL constructs like SKIP LOCKED). He agreed they cannot handle big data.

questions.q: Summarise the progression from approach 0 to approach 5.
questions.answer: First show the system fails (no checks, random seat, first free seat without locks), then ensure correctness with an exclusive lock (FOR UPDATE), then add SKIP LOCKED for performance, each step changing only two or three words.

questions.q: What phrase did the teacher ask you to remember for life, and how does the check-in problem map to it?
questions.answer: Fixed inventory + contention = locking. Fixed inventory: 120 seats; contention: 120 people trying to book them at once; so you must take locks to keep the system correct.

questions.q: Which similar fixed-inventory-plus-contention systems were listed?
questions.answer: CoWIN / COVID vaccination portal (limited hospital slots), IRCTC train booking, BookMyShow movie seats, and flash sales.

questions.q: For the COVID portal, how might they have implemented the slot booking?
questions.answer: With some form of locking: maybe pessimistic, maybe optimistic, maybe atomic instructions; on a relational DB you would do exactly what the demo did.

questions.q: What did the teacher say about IRCTC and BookMyShow in terms of locks?
questions.answer: IRCTC: under massive contention, high throughput needs skip locks, so their code base would be full of skip locks (and exclusive locks); without skip lock throughput would collapse. BookMyShow: exclusive lock, one who gets it moves forward, others wait for the transaction to complete.

questions.q: Is row locking implemented at the disk level? How is it implemented?
questions.answer: No, not at the disk level: in the database engine, on the CPU side, with mutexes or semaphores (in some cases monitors); otherwise atomic instructions. There is no other construct.

questions.q: How is holding a seat for ~10 minutes while the user pays handled? Is it a SQL lock?
questions.answer: It is not a SQL lock: you never keep a database transaction open until payment completes, which would drastically drop the SQL server's throughput. You take the lock only for a moment to mark the seat 'on hold' and split the flow into phases; 'hold' is the better word. Covered later with flash sale design.

questions.q: When users pick a specific seat (BookMyShow-style), should you use SKIP LOCKED? What does the losing transaction see?
questions.answer: No SKIP LOCKED; use FOR UPDATE on that seat (WHERE trip_id = 1 AND user_id IS NULL AND id = 67). One transaction succeeds; the other waits, re-evaluates and finds no rows matched, and the front end shows that the seat is gone.

questions.q: How did the teacher suggest exploring FOR SHARE / FOR UPDATE behaviour yourself?
questions.answer: Open two MySQL client terminals on the same server, set autocommit to 0, begin a transaction in each, take shared and exclusive locks and watch which statement halts and which moves; you will also discover deadlocks.

questions.q: With SKIP LOCKED, if the transaction that locked seat 2 fails, is seat 2 lost?
questions.answer: No. Rows are not assigned by position; whenever any transaction (re-)evaluates the query, a row that still matches (user_id null, order by id) is picked, so seat 2 will be taken by a later read. No row is skipped altogether.

questions.q: What did the teacher recommend for building deep understanding of database internals?
questions.answer: Dedicate about a week to reading the MySQL source code (C/C++), where terms like signals come from; official documentation always rules over YouTube videos.

questions.q: Without SKIP LOCKED, how many query evaluations happen in the worst case for N transactions, and why?
questions.answer: N(N+1)/2: after each commit all waiting transactions re-evaluate and one succeeds, so N + (N-1) + (N-2) + ... = N(N+1)/2.

questions.q: If you fire only an UPDATE (no SELECT ... FOR UPDATE), what governs concurrent behaviour, and how do you take a lock explicitly?
questions.answer: You never acquired a lock explicitly, so the transaction isolation level decides (serializable runs one after another; repeatable read and read committed each behave their own way). To lock explicitly, run SELECT ... FOR UPDATE first and then the UPDATE.

questions.q: Where does the demo code release (unlock) the locks it took?
questions.answer: Nowhere explicitly: committing the transaction (or aborting it) releases all its locks.

questions.q: When a lock is released, how do the waiting transactions find out? Is it a busy loop checking the lock?
questions.answer: No busy loop: thread signalling. Waiting threads sit on a wait queue and are signalled when the lock is released; OS fundamentals taught in college.

questions.q: Before the break, which generic claims about relational databases did the teacher say never to believe?
questions.answer: That relational databases don't scale / only non-relational ones scale / you can't partition them. You can do partitioning, sharding, everything on relational databases.

questions.q: How should you approach a problem labelled 'distributed'?
questions.answer: Don't design it to be distributed on day zero: implement a single-node version first, sort out its details, then scale out. Don't jump straight to leader election, Paxos or Raft.

questions.q: What are the KV store's requirements, and which real system is built this way?
questions.answer: Infinitely scalable; supports GET, PUT, DEL (delete) and TTL (auto expiration). Apache Ignite, a popular key-value store built on a relational DB.

questions.q: Which parts did the brainstorm cover, in the order listed on the board?
questions.answer: Storage, optimize storage, insert, update, TTL.

questions.q: What type was chosen for the key column, and why does the key's type matter so much?
questions.answer: Key is the primary key, e.g. varchar(16). The type determines what kind and size of keys the system supports, and once fixed you cannot change it, so know your requirements; as a database designer you must always care about storage size.

questions.q: What determines the value column's type, and what was chosen here?
questions.answer: Not what you store but how it is accessed. If users query inside the value (e.g. attributes of a JSON document, as in MongoDB), you need a type that supports it (e.g. MySQL's JSON type). Here the store is queried only by key and the value is a black box, so a BLOB (or varchar / long text) is used.

questions.q: What annotations were drawn next to the key and value columns of the store table?
questions.answer: key -> PK (varchar(16)); value -> (BLOB).

questions.q: What was the first proposal for supporting key-specific TTL?
questions.answer: Add created_at and ttl_sec columns, and a job that deletes rows where now() - created_at >= ttl.

questions.q: Why is DELETE ... WHERE now() - created_at >= ttl 'the worst query you can write'?
questions.answer: It is a dynamic computation per row, so no index can be used; every run has to scan every single row.

questions.q: How was the TTL design fixed so the cleanup query is efficient?
questions.answer: Don't store created_at and TTL; at write time store the absolute expiry time expired_at, index it, and the job runs DELETE FROM store WHERE expired_at <= now(), an efficient indexed query.

questions.q: What was the first soft-delete design proposed, and what did it require?
questions.answer: Add an is_deleted column set to true on delete, plus a second background job DELETE FROM store WHERE is_del = true; so two background jobs (one for expired, one for deleted).

questions.q: How is delete implemented in the final design?
questions.answer: As an update: UPDATE store SET expired_at = -1 WHERE key = k, using -1 as a special value marking deletion.

questions.q: Why does marking deletes with expired_at = -1 make the background job elegant?
questions.answer: One query, DELETE FROM store WHERE expired_at <= now(), matches both expired keys and soft-deleted (-1) keys: one job instead of two, no extra column, less CPU, disk and storage, and it uses the expired_at index.

questions.q: What was the plain insert proposed for PUT?
questions.answer: INSERT INTO store VALUES (k, v, e): key, value and expired_at.

questions.q: Why does a plain INSERT fail for 'put k1 v1' followed by 'put k1 v2'?
questions.answer: key is the primary key, so the second insert with the same key fails (key already exists), while a put is expected to replace the value.

questions.q: Why is 'GET the key, then UPDATE if it exists else INSERT' a bad way to implement put?
questions.answer: Every put becomes a get plus a write: an extra network round trip and a transaction wrapped around both, which is expensive and slows the system's throughput.

questions.q: What is an upsert and why is it better?
questions.answer: Insert if the key does not exist, update if it does, as one atomic SQL statement. The database checks existence itself, so you save the network I/O of bringing the row to the API server and avoid a big transaction around get+write; it keeps the database load minimal and throughput high.

questions.q: Which statements give upsert behaviour in Postgres and in MySQL?
questions.answer: Postgres: an upsert statement. MySQL: REPLACE INTO, or INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE.

questions.q: A student proposed fetching the key and checking expiry in the API server. Why is that wasteful?
questions.answer: You transfer the whole value (e.g. 10 MB) from the database to the API server only to discover it has expired.

questions.q: What GET query was written, and what does its extra clause save?
questions.answer: SELECT * FROM store WHERE key = k AND expired_at > now(). Expired values are never read out of the database, saving heavy network I/O, especially for big values.

questions.q: What storage choice and starting setup did the summary notes give?
questions.answer: MySQL; start with a single node and then scale as the system demands.

questions.q: What did the teacher say about the habitual auto-increment ID column?
questions.answer: You don't always need it; people add it out of habit because ORMs make life simple with it. Add it only if you actually need it.

questions.q: How does the final schema save storage compared with key | value | ttl | is_deleted?
questions.answer: Drop the is_deleted column and use the special value -1 in ttl (absolute expiration time) to mark deletion, leaving key, value, ttl.

questions.q: How are rows hard deleted, and why that way?
questions.answer: Batch and periodic cleanup: a separate process hard deletes the soft-deleted (and expired) rows in batches, which minimizes I/O and B+ tree rebalancing.

questions.q: According to the notes, what are the two cases when inserting a new key/value, and what is used instead of GET + INSERT/UPDATE?
questions.answer: 1. key exists -> update; 2. key does not exist -> insert. Use UPSERTS: REPLACE INTO 'store' VALUES (k, v, ttl) in MySQL; an UPSERT statement in PostgreSQL.

questions.q: How did the teacher suggest handling multiple concurrent PUT requests on the same key?
questions.answer: Leverage the database's locks (or isolation levels): locks protect data integrity, when one is updating the other waits; e.g. SELECT * FROM store ... FOR UPDATE NOWAIT, then UPDATE store SET value = v2 WHERE key = k1. NOWAIT vs SKIP LOCKED vs waiting depends on the guarantees you want; NOWAIT was just an example.

questions.q: Describe TTL approach 1 and the timeline drawn for it (D-07).
questions.answer: Batch deletion with a CRON job: on a timeline the job fires every t minutes (e.g. every 10 minutes) and hard deletes: DELETE FROM store WHERE expired_at < now().

questions.q: With cron deletion, what about expired keys read before the job runs, and what does the fix save?
questions.answer: They still exist, so GET must filter them out: SELECT * FROM store WHERE key = k AND ttl > now(). It saves the server's and the database's network bandwidth and the DB's disk I/O for reading a huge value.

questions.q: What is lazy deletion (TTL approach 2), and for which kind of database is it suitable?
questions.answer: For in-memory databases such as Redis: when a key that is accessed is found expired, it is hard deleted there and then (freed from the hash table) and reported as not existing.

questions.q: Why is pointed (lazy) deletion fine in memory but not for a disk-based database?
questions.answer: In memory it is just freeing a hash-table entry: no restructuring, no network I/O, microseconds. On disk every pointed delete requires B+ tree rebalancing, which is pathetically slow, so disk DBs delete in batches.

questions.q: What problem remains if you rely on lazy deletion alone?
questions.answer: A key that is never fetched is never deleted, so you still need a periodic (CRON) job to delete expired keys.

questions.q: Why doesn't Redis's periodic job just delete all expired keys on every run?
questions.answer: With millions of expired keys that would take a lot of time; lazy deletion already handles about 90% of the cleanup because expired keys are very likely to be accessed.

questions.q: List the steps of Redis's random sampling expiry (TTL approach 3) in the board's order.
questions.answer: 1. Randomly sample 20 keys that have an expiration set; 2. delete all the keys in the sample that are expired; 3. if the deleted keys are more than 25% of the sample, repeat the process; otherwise stop.

questions.q: What is the statistical idea behind the 25% threshold?
questions.answer: A random sample represents the population: if the sample has under 25% expired keys, the population has under 25% expired-but-not-deleted keys, which is acceptable, so the process stops.

questions.q: In one iteration, 3 of the 20 sampled keys are expired. What happens next?
questions.answer: Those 3 are deleted; 3/20 = 15% is below 25%, so the process stops; about 15% of the population may be expired but not deleted, which is accepted.

questions.q: What does Redis trade off with this expiry design, and why?
questions.answer: Speed over completeness: Redis is single-threaded, so time spent cleaning is time not spent serving get/put/delete commands. It accepts some memory held by expired keys (statistically at most about 20-25%, worst case), relying on lazy deletion plus random sampling.

questions.q: Why exactly 20 keys, and up to what scale was it said to work?
questions.answer: The sample size 20 comes from the Central Limit Theorem (proof in a paper linked from Redis's site); it works up to about 5 million keys.

questions.q: What is the delete micro-optimization, and what does it save?
questions.answer: UPDATE store SET ttl = -1 WHERE key = k1 AND ttl > NOW(). If the key is already expired the update matches no row, so no disk write happens: it saves two disk I/Os (the row and the ttl index), reducing the load on disk. Found in Apache Ignite's source.

questions.q: Write the three final queries for delete, batch cleanup and get.
questions.answer: Delete: UPDATE store SET ttl = -1 WHERE key = k1 AND ttl > NOW(); batch cleanup: DELETE FROM store WHERE ttl <= now() (removes expired and soft-deleted rows); get: SELECT * FROM store WHERE key = k1 AND ttl > NOW().

questions.q: Why set ttl to -1 on delete instead of relying on the stored expiry time?
questions.answer: A key may have no TTL and would never expire; when a user explicitly deletes a key you must record something in the DB, so you set a magic value (-1, or e.g. a date before 1 January 1970) that the cleanup query matches.

questions.q: What was the response to adding an in-memory append-only layer in front of the database to reduce insert I/O?
questions.answer: That is essentially adding a cache; all keys must fit in memory and it needs flushing. Such performance additions are possible but are not the core transactional database.

questions.q: Why does the KV store need to become distributed, and what does the single-node architecture (D-08) look like?
questions.answer: When one node can't handle the load (query volume, data size, network or disk I/O). Single node: user -> load balancer -> several KV API servers -> one MySQL, plus a separate periodic Batch Cleanup job against MySQL.

questions.q: What is the first thing you scale when load grows, and on what assumption? What do you check next?
questions.answer: Add more KV API servers, assuming MySQL can handle the incoming load. If it can't, look at the access pattern: are reads or updates/upserts/deletes dominating?

questions.q: When do you add read replicas, and which operations go to the master versus a replica (D-09)?
questions.answer: When reads dominate (e.g. read:write = 99:1), one DB can't handle them, and reading stale data is OK. Writes, deletes and consistent reads go to the master; stale-tolerant reads can go to replicas (replicated asynchronously). The KV API keeps connections to both; batch cleanup runs on the master.

questions.q: What do you do when the master can no longer handle the writes?
questions.answer: First vertically scale it up; if it still cannot handle the load, partition (shard) the data.

questions.q: Describe the partitioned architecture (D-10).
questions.answer: User -> load balancer -> KV API servers; every KV API connects to Master 1 holding keys [a-m] and Master 2 holding [n-z]. Each master owns an exclusive fragment of the data, has its own replica(s) and its own Batch Cleanup job.

questions.q: Who holds the routing information in the sharded KV store, and where would requests for 'Google' and 'Zomato' go?
questions.answer: The KV API servers store the key ranges and pick the database connection. 'Google' starts with G, so it goes to master 1 (a-m); 'Zomato' goes to master 2 (n-z).

questions.q: Why is static range-based sharding with routing in the API enough for most systems?
questions.answer: Around 90% of sharded databases work like this: dynamically adding or removing shards is rarely needed and is typically a one-time activity (about once a quarter) done explicitly, e.g. splitting the range into three when two nodes are not enough. Hot partitions and consistent hashing come later.

questions.q: What hands-on exercise did the teacher recommend for the distributed KV store?
questions.answer: Locally run two MySQL servers and one API server that connects to both, write the routing logic once behind an HTTP endpoint; as a stretch add a replica (MySQL binlog / Postgres log) and route critical reads to the master and others to the replica. No cloud needed.

questions.q: Why does the user delete query use ttl > now() while the batch cleanup uses ttl <= now()?
questions.answer: They are different operations: a user delete soft-deletes a key that has not yet expired (ttl is the absolute expiration time, e.g. 12 o'clock on a day), setting it to -1; batch cleanup hard deletes keys already expired or soft-deleted.

questions.q: For a key that is already expired, what happens when a user delete with the ttl > now() clause runs?
questions.answer: The update matches no row, so nothing is written to disk; the expired key is anyway removed by batch cleanup.

questions.q: Does the KV store keep ACID guarantees once it is partitioned?
questions.answer: Operations are key-based, so ACID holds per key, and within a shard (as long as all keys of an operation are on the same node). Across partitions you cannot have ACID; distributed transactions reduce performance hugely, so you typically don't do them.

questions.q: How should you mock a distributed system on a local machine?
questions.answer: Focus on the things that matter: one database and one replica running locally with an app server; skip autoscaling and the like.

questions.q: Is Redis's 25% condition about expired keys or deleted keys, and on what set?
questions.answer: About the keys deleted from the sample (the expired ones in the sample are deleted); it works only on the 20-key sample, never on the whole database, which may have millions of expired keys.

questions.q: Why should random sampling not be used for expiry in a disk-based database?
questions.answer: Picking 20 random rows means 20 random disk I/Os (pages anywhere on disk), which is very slow, plus deletes need rebalancing; it is better to skim the rows and batch-delete what is expired.

questions.q: With autocommit = true, do you still need an explicit transaction for SELECT ... FOR UPDATE?
questions.answer: Autocommit only commits standalone statements; inside BEGIN ... END the transaction commits at the end, so locks are held until then. To keep the lock across select and update, wrap them in a transaction.

questions.q: Is the N(N+1)/2 figure a count of queries the client fires?
questions.answer: No: it counts evaluations of the query done internally by the database, not queries fired by the client.

questions.q: Why does SKIP LOCKED need only about N evaluations even with ORDER BY id LIMIT 1?
questions.answer: The database never reads just one row: it reads a disk page / B+ tree node holding hundreds of rows; seeing the first row locked, it immediately moves to the next one without re-evaluating the query.

questions.q: At what point in query execution is LIMIT applied?
questions.answer: At the last step, when results are being accumulated; the rows are read and filtered first.

questions.q: What reasons did the teacher give for disliking ORMs?
questions.answer: They don't always generate optimal queries and are bad at advanced SQL; poor support for stored procedures; they select all columns by default; optimized ORM code becomes unreadable compared with plain SQL; they target general use across databases so DB-specific constructs are unsupported; connection handling/pooling problems.

questions.q: When is using an ORM fine?
questions.answer: At startups / early stage and mid-scale, where shipping velocity matters; don't over-optimize there. At high scale, where you need control and micro-optimizations, avoid them.

questions.q: Is writing native SQL queries inside an ORM for complex cases a good compromise?
questions.answer: Yes, 100%: ORMs don't give raw performance or DB-specific operations, and complex queries (joins of 10-15 tables, aggregations) are unreadable in ORM form but clear in SQL.

questions.q: Why did the teacher favour Go (and Python/C++) over Java?
questions.answer: Readable, sequential code without magic bean/dependency injection and abstraction layers (cf. FizzBuzz Enterprise Edition); better concurrency; minimal garbage collection time; the JVM takes ~200 MB just to start.

questions.q: What 'circle of life' of programming languages did the teacher describe?
questions.answer: Everyone starts fresh with a new language, over time it gets messy and people move to something new (JavaScript -> TypeScript, same will happen with Go and Rust): a language either dies a hero or lives long enough to become enterprise code.

questions.q: Why is 'SELECT TOP 1 1 ... then INSERT or UPDATE' still worse than an upsert?
questions.answer: Although it avoids reading a big value, it still needs two network round trips (four trips: request/response for the check, request/response for the write) versus one for an upsert; network time dominates, not DB evaluation time. Many systems just forget upsert exists.

questions.q: What causes 'lock wait timeout exceeded; try restarting transaction'?
questions.answer: A transaction waited too long for a lock because the transaction holding it neither committed nor aborted in the stipulated time: either it is doing very long processing (then increase the timeout) or it forgot to commit/abort.

questions.q: Why not hard delete the row right away instead of setting -1 and batch cleaning?
questions.answer: Every pointed delete can push the B+ tree out of shape and require rebalancing, which is expensive; so almost all databases do soft deletes plus batch cleanup.

questions.q: Why doesn't Redis hand off deleting an expired key it just read to a later job?
questions.answer: Freeing an object in the in-memory hash table is very lightweight (microseconds, no B+ tree rebalancing); delegating could cost more, and freeing immediately releases memory so new data can be inserted when Redis is near full capacity.

questions.q: For an online/offline indicator, why can't the server push/poll the user?
questions.answer: The server does not know the user's IP address until the user opens a connection to it; you cannot establish a TCP connection to a machine without its IP. The user knows the server's address, so the user connects.

questions.q: Why might WhatsApp Web show no heartbeat requests?
questions.answer: It uses a WebSocket: the existence of the connection is the presence signal (connected = online, terminated = offline), so no explicit heartbeat is needed. With WebSockets disabled you might see explicit heartbeat calls.

questions.q: Are real KV stores built on a relational database like this?
questions.answer: Redis no (in-memory store); DynamoDB no; Apache Ignite yes, something very similar. The relational DB was used to teach micro-optimizations; real stores replace it with their own storage layer (e.g. LSM tree, covered later).

questions.q: Why did the teacher refuse to share the demo code?
questions.answer: He wants students to write it themselves and make mistakes (deadlocks, low throughput) and learn from fixing them; that makes better engineers.

questions.q: Why don't relational databases provide soft deletion out of the box?
questions.answer: The database is a foundational layer: it gives basic building blocks (FOR UPDATE, FOR SHARE, SKIP LOCKED, NOWAIT) and does not intrude on the user's space; knowing what not to build matters. Soft delete would also need a cleanup process and add cognitive load for developers. Key-value stores like DynamoDB do soft delete since for them it is foundational.

questions.q: For the previous week's blogging assignment, should students build a front end?
questions.answer: No: implement only what you want to learn (APIs with short/long polling, put and consume messages on Kafka or RabbitMQ), as the airline demo did; don't waste time on front end.
